Silver mountain voles (Alticola argentatus) inhabiting the high-altitude rocky slopes of Central Asia exhibit a compact, high-metabolism life history finely tuned to their cold and unproductive environment. Their neonates are exceptionally small at birth, with newborn pups weighing just three grams [Wwb = three grams], a value inferred from the closely related Alticola strelzowi. This diminutive birth mass is paired with a very brief gestation period of twenty days [tg = twenty days] when measured at a standard body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that is among the shortest documented for arvicoline rodents of comparable adult size. The rapid foetal development is likely an adaptation to the short, resource-limited growing season typical of alpine habitats. Consequently, pups are born in a highly altricial state, requiring intensive maternal investment during the initial days of life.

Weaning occurs relatively early in this species, with nutritional independence achieved at just seventeen days after birth [tx = seventeen days after birth] under the thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This early transition to solid food corresponds with a rapid juvenile growth phase, a necessity in environments where the window for reaching reproductive condition is brief. Despite the early weaning, juveniles do not attain sexual maturity quickly. Field and captive data from congeneric species indicate that puberty is not reached until ninety-six days since birth [tp = ninety-six days since birth] at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This substantial lag between weaning and reproductive maturation suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth necessary for surviving the harsh winter conditions.

Adult females typically produce litters containing 3.6 pups [N_R_i = litters containing 3.6 pups], and given the short alpine summers, available data indicate they achieve approximately 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 litters per year], resulting in a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 9 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 9 offspring per year]. This collective annual reproductive output supports population stability in the face of high overwinter mortality. The relatively modest litter size is balanced by the extended breeding window afforded by a flexible reproductive schedule, allowing females to carefully time parturition with peak resource availability in the short mountain summer.

The ultimate body mass of a fully grown adult is reported to reach up to 54.6 grams [Wwi = up to 54.6 grams], though a range of 20.8 to 54.6 (20.8-54.6 grams [Wwi = 20.8-54.6 grams]) grams has been observed across different populations, likely reflecting local variation in resource quality and elevation. This modest size, combined with the challenges of thermoregulation at altitude, places a strong energetic demand on the vole. Basal oxygen consumption measurements reveal a maximum resting metabolic rate of 127 milliliters per hour [JOi = 127 milliliters per hour] when assessed at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Such a high mass-specific metabolic rate is characteristic of small endotherms living in cold climates, enabling them to maintain core body temperature despite severe thermal gradients.

Longevity in these high-elevation rodents is surprisingly extended for their body size. The maximum lifespan has been recorded at approximately 3.3 years [am = approximately 3.3 years], a figure calculated from field mark-recapture studies assuming continuous activity at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] which equates to roughly 1205 days. This relatively long lifespan is notable because it exceeds predictions based on body size alone for most microtine rodents. The combination of a moderate reproductive rate with an extended adult survival period suggests a bet-hedging strategy, where individuals buffer against years of reproductive failure by surviving and breeding across multiple seasons in their harsh, unpredictable alpine environment.
